summary: The Chiropractic Board of Australia sets the standards for clinical practice,  record-keeping, and advertising for chiropractors under the National Registration  and Accreditation Scheme.
longSummary:
The Chiropractic Board of Australia (CBA) is the national regulator responsible for 
protecting the public by ensuring that chiropractors are registered, qualified, 
and competent to practise. The Board develops standards, codes, and guidelines 
that define the professional and ethical expectations for the profession, 
including the Code of Conduct for Registered Health Practitioners.

Clinical records are a critical component of professional accountability. The Board 
requires that records be contemporaneous, accurate, and sufficiently detailed to 
support the clinical reasoning behind every diagnosis and treatment intervention. 
This includes documenting spinal screening results, imaging justifications, 
informed consent, and the specific adjustment techniques used. Records must be 
maintained in a way that ensures patient safety and continuity of care, and 
must be readily available for audit or in the event of a complaint.

Salvia integrates these regulatory requirements directly into the clinical 
workflow. By structuring intake assessments, treatment plans, and session notes 
to include mandatory fields like clinical rationale and outcome measures, Salvia 
ensures that practitioners meet the Board’s expectations for evidence-based 
practice and documentation. The platform’s audit trail provides the necessary 
transparency for compliance with the National Law.

summary: The Dental Board of Australia, under AHPRA, mandates strict standards for clinical documentation, radiograph justification, and informed consent for all dental practitioners.

The Dental Board of Australia (DBA) is the statutory body responsible for regulating dental practitioners in Australia under the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law. The Board sets the standards, codes, and guidelines that all dental practitioners must meet to ensure safe and effective patient care. This includes the Code of Conduct, which dictates the ethical obligations of practitioners, and the Guidelines for Dental Records, which define the requirements for clinical documentation.

Compliance requires that records be contemporaneous, accurate, and legible, serving as a reliable account of the patient's care. The Board specifically mandates that medical history be reviewed at every appointment, BPE scoring be performed at every recall, and that soft tissue examinations are conducted for oral cancer screening. Furthermore, the Board requires strict adherence to the ARPANSA Code of Practice regarding the justification of radiographs at the time of exposure, and that all treatment plans are provided in writing with itemised costs and signed by the patient prior to the commencement of treatment.

Salvia ensures compliance by structuring clinical notes to force the inclusion of these mandatory elements. By integrating the ARPANSA justification requirements and the DBA's record-keeping standards into the SOAP note and treatment planning workflows, Salvia provides an audit-ready environment that captures the necessary clinical reasoning, attribution, and patient consent, ensuring that every record meets the high standards expected by the Dental Board of Australia.

summary: ARPANSA's Radiation Protection Series No. 10 and state radiation protection legislation require that every dental radiograph is clinically justified, exposure minimised, and findings documented. Compliance is enforced by state radiation health authorities.
longSummary:
The Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Agency (ARPANSA) publishes the Radiation Protection Series No. 10 (RPS No. 10) — the national guidance standard for radiation protection in dentistry. State and territory radiation health authorities (e.g., NSW Health, DHHS Victoria) legislate the requirements and conduct audits. Dental practitioners and practices must comply with both the national guidance and their state radiation legislation.

**Justification:**
Every radiograph must be individually clinically justified before exposure. Justification must be documented in the patient record at the time of the decision. Routine "surveillance" radiographs without clinical indication are not compliant.

**Exposure minimisation (ALARA):**
Exposures must be kept As Low As Reasonably Achievable (ALARA). Film type, equipment settings, and technique must be optimised. RVGs (digital sensors) are preferred over film for dose reduction.

**Documentation requirements:**
For each radiographic exposure, the patient record must contain:
- Date and type of radiograph
- Clinical justification
- Radiographic findings and interpretation
- Dentist name and signature

**Radiation Use Licences:**
State legislation requires dental practices to hold a current Radiation Use Licence. The dentist supervising radiographs must hold the appropriate licence. Licence details must be available during inspection.

**Retention:**
Radiographic records must be retained as part of the patient record for the period required by state health records legislation — generally 7 years for adults, and until the patient is 25 for records created when the patient was a minor.

fullName: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners — Standards for General Practices (5th Edition)
summary: The RACGP Standards (5th edition) are used for accreditation of Australian GP practices. Health record standards (Criterion C1.1) require structured, contemporaneous, attributable records, secure storage, and privacy-compliant access controls.
longSummary:
The Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP) publishes the Standards for General Practices, now in its 5th edition. These standards are used by accreditation bodies (AGPAL, QPA) to assess general practices for accreditation, which is required for PIP (Practice Incentives Program) eligibility. Accreditation status directly affects practice revenue through government incentives.

**Criterion C1.1 — Health records:**
Practices must have documented systems for managing health records. Requirements:
- Records must be created at the time of the consultation or immediately after
- Every entry must be attributable to the clinician who created it, with date and time
- Records must include: presenting complaint, history, examination findings, risk factors, investigations ordered and results, diagnosis, management plan, prescriptions, referrals, and follow-up
- Transfer and communication records (specialist letters, discharge summaries) must be filed in the patient record

**Privacy and access:**
Health records must comply with the Privacy Act 1988 and Australian Privacy Principles (APPs). Records must be stored securely. Access is limited to treating clinicians. Patients have the right to access their records.

**Electronic health records:**
Digital records must meet the same standards as paper records. Backup, disaster recovery, and access control requirements must be documented. Audit logs must be available.

**Retention:**
Records must be retained for 7 years from the date of last entry, or until age 25 for records created when the patient was under 18.

**Shared care:**
Where patients are under the care of multiple providers, the practice must have a system for sharing relevant information and maintaining a complete record.

summary: State and territory Veterinary Practitioners Boards (VPBs) in NSW, VIC, QLD, WA, SA, TAS, and ACT administer registration, conduct investigations, and inspect clinical records for compliance with state-level veterinary practice legislation.
longSummary:
Australia has no single national veterinary regulator. Each state and territory operates a Veterinary Practitioners Board (or equivalent) under its own legislation. The major boards are:

- **NSW**: Veterinary Practitioners Board of NSW (Veterinary Practice Act 2003)
- **VIC**: Veterinary Practitioners Registration Board of Victoria (Veterinary Practice Act 1997)
- **QLD**: Queensland Veterinary Surgeons Board (Veterinary Surgeons Act 1936)
- **WA**: Veterinary Surgeons' Board of Western Australia (Veterinary Chemical Control and Animal Feeding Stuffs Act 1976)
- **SA**: Veterinary Practice Board of South Australia (Veterinary Practice Act 2003)

Despite different legislation, the practical record-keeping obligations are consistent across all states:

**Clinical records:** Must be contemporaneous, legible, and include: patient ID, owner details, date, presenting complaint, clinical findings, diagnosis, treatment, drugs administered, and follow-up. Retention varies by state but is 5–7 years.

**Controlled drugs:** All states require a drug register consistent with the relevant Drugs, Poisons, and Controlled Substances Act. Schedule 8 (equivalent to UK Schedule 2) requires register entries, witness signatures, and running balance.

**Inspections:** Board inspectors may visit practices unannounced to inspect records, drug registers, and facilities. Digital records must be immediately accessible and legible during inspection.

Salvia's exportable, audit-ready record system meets the practical inspection requirements of all state VPBs.

fullName: Competition and Markets Authority — Veterinary Services Remedies 2026
summary: Twenty-one binding remedies from the CMA's 2024 Veterinary Services Market Investigation. Core compliance obligations: upfront price display, written estimates before treatment, prescription transparency, complaints logging, and itemised invoicing.
longSummary:
The CMA's Veterinary Services Market Investigation concluded in 2024 with a Final Report finding that weak consumer engagement and limited transparency were causing detriment in the UK veterinary market. The remedies became binding from September 2026 under an Order. All UK veterinary practices — regardless of size or corporate ownership — must comply.

The records-implicated obligations are:
- **Written estimates**: A written (including digital) estimate must be provided to the client before any procedure. The estimate must itemise services and drugs at the practice's current prices.
- **Price transparency**: Standard prices for consultations, common treatments, and drugs must be published on the practice website and made available in practice.
- **Prescription transfers**: If a client requests a written prescription, the practice must provide it at a fair price. The practice cannot condition a prescription on purchasing medicines from the practice.
- **Complaint records**: Practices must maintain a written complaints procedure and log every complaint and its resolution, retaining records for at least 3 years.
- **Out-of-hours transparency**: Clients must be told at registration which provider handles out-of-hours care and the associated price differential.
- **Data portability**: Pet owners must be able to obtain their pet's clinical records in a usable format within 10 working days of request.

Salvia supports compliance by generating itemised digital estimates linked to treatment plans, capturing client acknowledgement, maintaining a searchable complaint log via the incident register, and exporting full clinical records on demand.

fullName: Veterinary Medicines Regulations 2013 (as amended) — United Kingdom
summary: The VMR governs prescribing, dispensing, administration, and disposal of veterinary medicines in the UK, including controlled drug register requirements for Schedule 2 and 3 substances. Non-compliance is a criminal offence.
longSummary:
The Veterinary Medicines Regulations 2013 (SI 2013/2033), administered by the Veterinary Medicines Directorate (VMD), establish the legal framework for all veterinary medicines used in the UK. Key categories relevant to clinical records:

**Prescribing categories:**
- **POM-V** (Prescription Only Medicine — Veterinarian): must be prescribed in person after clinical examination; written prescription required.
- **POM-VPS**: may be prescribed by a veterinarian, pharmacist, or SQP; written record required.
- **NFA-VPS / AVM-GSL**: non-prescription categories, but all administration must still be recorded.

**Controlled Drugs (CDs):**
Schedule 2 and 3 CDs require a register maintained in chronological order, including: date, client name and address, drug name/form/strength, quantity, batch number, and witness signature for Schedule 2. The register must be retained for 5 years and kept at the practice premises. Running balance must be maintained and reconciled at least monthly.

**Retention:** All prescription records must be kept for 5 years. The CD register must be kept for 5 years after the date of the last entry.

Salvia's drug register enforces witness capture, running balance reconciliation, and retains all entries in the immutable audit log for the required 5-year period.

longSummary:
The Dental Council of Ireland regulates dentists and dental specialists under the Dentists Act 1985 (as amended). Registration with the Council is mandatory for all practising dentists in Ireland. The Council's Standards Guidance and supporting documents establish the clinical and ethical obligations of registered practitioners.

**Clinical record requirements:**
Records must be contemporaneous, accurate, legible, and retained for a minimum of 7 years (10 years if the patient was under 18 at the time of treatment, and until age 25 for a minor — whichever is longer). Records must include: patient demographics, medical history (updated every visit), clinical examination findings, treatment plan with costs, treatment delivered, and follow-up.

**Radiographs:**
Every radiograph must be clinically justified at the time of exposure. The justification must be documented in the patient record. Radiographic findings must be recorded and reported. Basic Periodontal Examination (BPE) scores must be recorded at every check-up.

**Consent:**
Informed consent must be obtained and documented before any irreversible procedure. The consent record must include: procedure name, risks and alternatives explained, and patient signature for complex or surgical procedures.

**Medical history:**
A full medical history must be taken and recorded at registration and updated (not merely "confirmed") at each subsequent visit.

**Data protection:**
Records are subject to GDPR and the Data Protection Acts 1988–2018. Subject access requests must be fulfilled within 30 days.

longSummary:

**Clinical record requirements:**
Records must be contemporaneous, accurate, and retained for a minimum of 8 years from the date of last entry (or until the patient is 25 years old for records created when the patient was under 18). Records must include: patient demographics, presenting complaint, history, examination findings, differential diagnosis, investigations ordered and results, treatment plan and rationale, prescriptions, follow-up, and any advice given. Every entry must be signed and dated.

**Prescribing:**
Prescriptions must be legible, dated, signed, and include the full drug name (not abbreviations), dose, frequency, and route. Prescribing decisions must be recorded with clinical rationale. Off-label use must be documented with justification.

**Consent:**
Informed consent must be obtained and documented before any procedure or course of treatment that carries material risk. The consent record must demonstrate that the patient was informed of diagnosis, treatment options, risks, benefits, and alternatives in terms the patient could understand.

**Referrals:**
All referrals must be documented, including clinical reason, urgency, and what information was shared with the receiving clinician.

**Data protection:**
Clinical records are subject to GDPR and the Health (Provision of Information) Act 1997. Patient records must be processed lawfully, stored securely, and made available for subject access requests within 30 days.

A unique health ID for every patient. Records can be linked to the patient's ABHA so they are portable and retrievable across facilities with consent.

ABDM is the rail that makes digital records portable and government-recognised. Producing structured, standards-aligned records is the precondition for linking to ABHA and participating in the exchange.

fullName: Central Government Health Scheme — Empanelment Conditions & Record Requirements
summary: The Central Government Health Scheme empanels private hospitals, clinics, dental and diagnostic centres to treat CGHS beneficiaries at notified package rates. Empanelment typically requires NABH/NABL accreditation and disciplined treatment, billing, and record documentation against CGHS rate lists.
longSummary:
The Central Government Health Scheme (CGHS) provides healthcare to central government employees, pensioners, and dependants. Private healthcare providers can be empanelled to serve CGHS beneficiaries, which is a significant revenue channel — but empanelment carries documentation and accreditation conditions.

**Accreditation as a gate:**
CGHS empanelment generally requires NABH (Entry-Level or full) accreditation for clinical facilities and NABL accreditation for labs. Accredited facilities also receive higher package rates than non-accredited ones.

**Package rates and billing:**
Treatment is reimbursed at CGHS-notified package rates. Providers must bill against the correct package, record the treatment delivered, and retain supporting clinical documentation for claims and audit.

**Records for claims:**
Each CGHS claim must be backed by complete treatment records, referrals, and discharge documentation. Discrepancies between billed packages and recorded treatment are a common audit failure.

**Why it matters:**
Empanelment revenue depends on accreditation plus clean, auditable records that match what was billed. Salvia's structured, retained records support both the accreditation gate and the claim documentation.

clauses.implication: Salvia's NABH-aligned, audit-ready records support the accreditation that gates CGHS empanelment and unlocks higher reimbursement.

fullName: Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010 & Rules
summary: The Clinical Establishments Act, 2010 requires registration of clinical establishments and adherence to minimum standards, including maintenance and reporting of patient records and electronic health records in the prescribed formats. It is adopted across many states and union territories.
longSummary:
The Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010 is the central legislation requiring every clinical establishment — clinics, polyclinics, dental establishments, labs, and hospitals — to be registered and to meet minimum standards of facilities and services. It has been adopted by numerous states and union territories, with several states running their own equivalent Acts.

**Registration and standards:**
Establishments must register with the State Council / District Registering Authority and comply with the minimum standards notified for their category. Conditions of registration include maintaining and providing records and statistics, and displaying rates.

**Records and EHR:**
A core condition is the maintenance of medical records of every patient and the maintenance of records of the establishment, increasingly required to be kept and reported in electronic health record (EHR) formats as notified. Establishments must furnish returns/information to the authority.

**Stabilisation and emergency:**
The Act obliges establishments to provide emergency medical care within their capacity and to document it.

**Why it matters:**
Registration is a legal prerequisite to operate in adopting states. Inspections check record-keeping. Salvia's structured, retrievable records directly support the record-maintenance conditions of registration.

fullName: Dentists Act, 1948 & Dental Council of India — Professional Conduct & Records
summary: The Dental Council of India, under the Dentists Act, 1948, regulates dental practice and professional conduct in India. Registered dentists must maintain proper clinical records, obtain informed consent, and prescribe responsibly — the dental analogue of the NMC conduct duties.
longSummary:
The Dental Council of India (DCI) is the statutory body constituted under the Dentists Act, 1948 that regulates dental education and the profession. DCI's professional-conduct regulations bind every registered dentist and set the baseline duties for clinical record-keeping and patient interaction.

**Clinical records:**
Registered dentists must maintain accurate clinical records of patients — history, examination, diagnosis, treatment provided, and outcome — and produce them when properly required.

**Informed consent:**
Consent must be obtained and documented for procedures, particularly invasive treatment, surgery, and use of anaesthesia/sedation.

**Prescriptions and conduct:**
Prescriptions must be appropriate and legible; the dentist must practise ethically and maintain confidentiality of patient information (now reinforced by the DPDP Act).

**Why it matters:**
Like the NMC for doctors, DCI conduct rules make record-keeping and consent a professional duty independent of accreditation. Incomplete or unavailable records are a conduct issue. Salvia's structured records and consent module satisfy these duties by default.

summary: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs the processing of digital personal data — including patient and client health data. It requires notice and consent, purpose limitation, security safeguards, breach notification, and honouring data-principal rights such as access, correction, and erasure.
longSummary:
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act) is India's omnibus data-protection law. A clinic, hospital, dental practice, or veterinary practice that processes personal data in digital form is a Data Fiduciary and must comply.

**Notice and consent:**
Personal data may be processed only for a lawful purpose with the consent of the Data Principal (patient/client), preceded by a clear notice describing the data collected and the purpose. Consent must be free, specific, informed, and revocable. (Salvia's design — no sensitive patient data leaves for the AI without consent — maps directly to this.)

**Purpose limitation and minimisation:**
Data may be used only for the purpose for which consent was given, and retained only as long as necessary for that purpose.

**Security safeguards:**
A Data Fiduciary must implement reasonable security safeguards to prevent personal data breaches, and must notify the Data Protection Board and affected Data Principals of a breach.

**Data-principal rights:**
Individuals have the right to access a summary of their data, seek correction or erasure, and grievance redressal.

**Why it matters:**
Health data is among the most sensitive personal data. DPDP applies regardless of accreditation status, and consent + breach + rights handling must be demonstrable.

fullName: National Accreditation Board for Hospitals & Healthcare Providers — Standards for Small Healthcare Organisations (SHCO) / Entry-Level Certification
summary: NABH accreditation is India's primary quality benchmark for clinics and hospitals. Its Information Management System (IMS) standards require complete, legible, contemporaneous medical records with documented consent, retention, and audit controls. NABH Entry-Level certification is a gatekeeper for CGHS empanelment and higher PM-JAY package rates.
longSummary:
The National Accreditation Board for Hospitals & Healthcare Providers (NABH), a constituent board of the Quality Council of India, sets the accreditation standards used across Indian healthcare. For clinics and small facilities, the relevant track is NABH Entry-Level Certification for Small Healthcare Organisations (SHCO), which is increasingly required for CGHS empanelment and unlocks higher reimbursement under PM-JAY.

**Information Management System (IMS) — medical records:**
NABH standards require that every patient has an accurate, complete, and legible medical record. Each entry must be dated, timed, and authenticated (signed/attributed) to the author. The record must capture the assessment, care plan, consent, procedures, medication, and outcome. Records must be stored securely with controlled access, and the organisation must define and enforce a retention period consistent with statutory norms.

**Consent:**
Documented informed consent is required for procedures and treatments carrying risk. Consent records must identify the procedure, the risks explained, and be signed by the patient (or guardian) and the clinician.

**Continuity and handover:**
The record must support continuity of care — referrals, discharge instructions, and follow-up must be documented and retrievable.

**Audit:**
NABH assessors review records for completeness and consistency during accreditation and surveillance visits. A maintainable audit trail of access and amendments is expected, which is precisely the manual burden that causes compliance to lapse after an audit.

fullName: NABH — Accreditation Standards for Dental Healthcare Service Providers

It applies the NABH quality philosophy to the dental setting and is a quality differentiator (and, like clinical NABH, supportive of empanelment).

**Dental records:**
Each patient must have a complete dental record: history, examination, dental charting, diagnosis, treatment plan, procedures performed, materials used, and outcome — dated, timed, and attributable to the treating dentist.

**Informed consent:**
Documented informed consent is required for invasive and risk-bearing dental procedures (extractions, surgery, implants, endodontics), identifying the procedure and risks explained.

**Infection control and radiation:**
Sterilisation/infection-control logs and dental radiography (AERB-aligned) documentation are part of the standards.

**Retention and access:**
Records must be retained per statutory norms and stored securely with controlled access.

fullName: National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories — Medical Testing (ISO 15189)
summary: NABL accredits medical and diagnostic laboratories in India against ISO 15189. It requires controlled documentation of the total testing process — request, sample identification, results, validation, and reporting — with traceability and retention. NABL accreditation is often a prerequisite for CGHS/PM-JAY lab empanelment.
longSummary:
The National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories (NABL), a constituent board of the Quality Council of India, accredits medical/diagnostic laboratories against ISO 15189 (Medical laboratories — requirements for quality and competence). For diagnostic and allied-health facilities, NABL accreditation evidences competence and is frequently required for empanelment under government schemes.

**Documentation of the testing process:**
Laboratories must control documents and records across the pre-analytical, analytical, and post-analytical phases: test request, patient/sample identification, chain of custody, results, validation/authorisation, and the final report.

**Traceability and authorisation:**
Each result must be traceable to the sample and authorised by a competent person before release. Amendments to reports must be controlled and identifiable.

**Retention:**
Records and reports must be retained for defined periods and be retrievable for audit and surveillance assessment.

**Why it matters:**
Lab/diagnostic records have strict traceability and authorisation requirements. Salvia's structured, attributable, retained records support the documentation discipline NABL assessors check.

fullName: National Commission for Allied and Healthcare Professions Act, 2021
summary: The NCAHP Act, 2021 establishes statutory regulation of allied and healthcare professionals in India — physiotherapists, occupational therapists, and others. Registered professionals must practise within their scope, maintain proper clinical records, and obtain documented consent for treatment.
longSummary:
The National Commission for Allied and Healthcare Professions Act, 2021 (NCAHP Act) created, for the first time, a statutory regulatory framework for allied and healthcare professions in India, including physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and many other disciplines. It establishes the National Commission and State Councils, professional registers, and standards of professional conduct.

**Registration and scope of practice:**
Professionals must be registered and practise within the defined scope for their category. Records should evidence that care was within scope.

**Clinical records:**
Registered professionals must maintain proper, contemporaneous clinical records of assessment, treatment plan, interventions, and outcomes, retrievable when required.

**Informed consent:**
Consent for assessment and treatment should be obtained and documented, particularly for hands-on or risk-bearing interventions.

**Professional conduct and confidentiality:**
Practitioners must adhere to the standards of professional conduct and protect patient information (reinforced by the DPDP Act).

**Why it matters:**
Allied health is now statutorily regulated in India. Proper records, scope evidence, and consent are professional duties. Salvia structures discipline-appropriate records and consent so allied professionals meet NCAHP duties without manual paperwork.

fullName: National Medical Commission — Registered Medical Practitioner (Professional Conduct) Regulations, 2023
summary: The NMC (successor to the Medical Council of India) sets the professional-conduct rules for registered medical practitioners in India. Practitioners must maintain medical records for at least 3 years, supply them to patients within a defined window, and prescribe legibly using generic names.
longSummary:
The National Medical Commission (NMC) replaced the Medical Council of India and issues the conduct regulations binding on every Registered Medical Practitioner (RMP) in India. The 2023 Registered Medical Practitioner (Professional Conduct) Regulations carry forward and modernise the record-keeping duties previously found in the MCI Code of Ethics Regulations, 2002.

**Medical records:**
An RMP must maintain the medical records of patients for a minimum of 3 years from the commencement of treatment. Where a patient or an authorised person requests records, the practitioner must supply them within a defined period (typically within 5 days). Records must be maintained in a documented, retrievable form.

**Prescriptions:**
Prescriptions must be legible, preferably typed/printed, and use generic drug names. The practitioner must record the diagnosis and treatment.

**Consent and documentation:**
The RMP must document informed consent for procedures and maintain truthful, contemporaneous notes. Tele-consultation records are held to the same standard under the telemedicine guidelines.

**Why it matters:**
These are the baseline statutory duties for every doctor in India — independent of accreditation. Failure to produce records on request, or illegible/incomplete records, is a conduct issue, not merely an accreditation gap.

fullName: Indian Veterinary Council Act, 1984 & Veterinary Council of India — Standards of Professional Conduct

Practitioners must keep proper case records, maintain a drug register for scheduled medicines, obtain owner consent, and prescribe responsibly.

The Veterinary Council of India (VCI) is the statutory body under the Indian Veterinary Council Act, 1984. Its Standards of Veterinary Professional Conduct regulations govern registered veterinary practitioners and set duties for case documentation, medicine handling, and client interaction.

**Case records:**
A practitioner must maintain proper clinical case records for animals treated — history, examination, diagnosis, treatment, and outcome — retrievable when required.

**Drug register and scheduled medicines:**
Veterinary use of scheduled drugs (under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rules, including Schedule H/H1 medicines) requires correct recording. Maintaining a drug register / dispensing record is a core compliance duty for practices that store and dispense medicines.

**Owner consent:**
Consent from the animal's owner/keeper should be obtained and documented for surgery, anaesthesia, and risk-bearing procedures.

**Confidentiality and conduct:**
Practitioners must act ethically and protect client information (owner personal data falls under the DPDP Act).

Vet practices carry the same record + drug-register + consent burden as human clinics, plus controlled-medicine duties. Salvia's structured records, consent module, and drug register remove the manual burden that causes these to lapse.

summary: The Chiropractic Board of New Zealand (CBNZ) sets the standards for ethical and professional conduct under the HPCA Act, requiring chiropractors to maintain accurate, contemporaneous, and secure clinical records.
longSummary:
The Chiropractic Board of New Zealand (CBNZ) is the statutory authority established under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance (HPCA) Act 2003. Its primary role is to protect the health and safety of the public by ensuring that all chiropractors are competent and fit to practise. The Board sets the Standards of Ethical and Professional Conduct, which mandate how clinical records must be maintained, stored, and protected to ensure continuity of care and professional accountability.

Under these standards, chiropractors are required to maintain detailed clinical records that include the patient's history, examination findings, clinical reasoning, diagnosis, treatment plans, and informed consent. Records must be contemporaneous, legible, and attributable to the specific practitioner. The Board emphasizes that clinical notes must be sufficient to allow another practitioner to understand the patient's condition and the rationale for the care provided, ensuring high standards of patient safety and professional integrity.

Salvia integrates these requirements by structuring clinical documentation to capture essential chiropractic data points, such as spinal screening results, imaging justifications, and specific adjustment techniques. By automating the inclusion of professional registration details and maintaining a robust audit trail, Salvia ensures that New Zealand chiropractors can demonstrate compliance with CBNZ standards during audits or in response to patient inquiries.

summary: The Medical Council of New Zealand (MCNZ) sets the standards for medical practice, requiring GPs to maintain clear, accurate, and contemporaneous records that ensure continuity of care and patient safety under the HPCA Act.
longSummary:
The Medical Council of New Zealand (MCNZ) is the statutory body responsible for ensuring that doctors are competent and fit to practise. Under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance (HPCA) Act 2003, the Council sets standards for clinical record-keeping, which are essential for patient safety, continuity of care, and professional accountability.

GPs are required to maintain records that are contemporaneous, legible, and attributable. These records must document the clinical history, examination findings, assessment, and the management plan (SOAP). Furthermore, the MCNZ mandates that doctors must obtain and document informed consent for procedures and maintain accurate prescribing logs, especially for controlled drugs.

Salvia integrates these requirements by enforcing structured SOAP note generation, mandatory attribution for locums and nursing staff, and a robust audit trail for all clinical entries. summary: AAHA accreditation is a voluntary but widely adopted quality standard for US small-animal veterinary practices. Standards cover clinical records, anaesthesia, surgery, pharmacy, dental, and pain management. Only ~15% of US practices are AAHA-accredited.
longSummary:
The American Animal Hospital Association (AAHA) is the only organisation in the US and Canada to accredit companion animal veterinary practices. Accreditation is voluntary but widely regarded as the gold standard for practice quality. Accredited practices undergo an initial on-site evaluation and renewal every 3 years.

AAHA evaluates over 900 standards across 18 modules. The records-implicated modules most relevant to Salvia:

**Medical Records (Module 1):**
Records must be complete, legible, problem-oriented, and contemporaneous. Required fields: patient signalment, owner contact, presenting complaint, history, physical examination, assessment, diagnosis, and treatment plan. All records must be attributed to the clinician with date and time. Records must be retained for 3 years minimum (5 years recommended).

**Anesthesia (Module 6):**
Anaesthesia records must capture: pre-anaesthetic assessment, ASA classification, drug protocol, monitoring parameters at timed intervals (minimum every 5 minutes), recovery notes, and clinician signature.

**Pharmacy (Module 14):**
A controlled drug log must be maintained for all DEA Schedule II–V drugs. Log entries: date, patient, drug, quantity, administering clinician, and witness. Discrepancy reporting to DEA is required.

**Dentistry (Module 8):**
Dental records must include: periodontal chart with probe depths, radiographic findings (whole-mouth radiographs required for dental procedures), assessment of each tooth, and treatment performed.

**Pain Management (Module 11):**
Pain assessment scores must be recorded at each visit. A validated pain scale must be used. Pain management plans must be documented.

Salvia supports AAHA accreditation preparation with structured digital records that satisfy Module 1, 6, 8, 11, and 14 documentation requirements.

fullName: American Veterinary Medical Association + American Animal Hospital Association
summary: The AVMA and AAHA set the national standards for veterinary medical records, controlled substance management, and clinical practice in the United States.
longSummary:
The American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA) provides the Principles of Veterinary Medical Ethics, while the American Animal Hospital Association (AAHA) establishes the Standards of Accreditation. Together, these bodies define the clinical and administrative requirements for veterinary practices, including the management of controlled substances under DEA 21 CFR 1304.

Veterinary records must be contemporaneous, legible, and identifiable, serving as a legal document of the care provided to the patient. Compliance requires meticulous tracking of patient identification, owner information, surgical and euthanasia consent, and detailed logs for anesthesia and analgesia. Controlled drug registers must be maintained with strict accountability, including witness verification and balance reconciliation.

Salvia integrates these requirements by structuring clinical workflows to ensure every SOAP note, treatment record, and drug entry is attributable to a specific practitioner. The system enforces the documentation of informed consent and provides the audit trails necessary for state practice act compliance and AAHA accreditation audits.

clauses.ref: AVMA Principles of Veterinary Medical Ethics
clauses.title: Medical Records
clauses.text: Veterinarians should maintain medical records that are legible, accurate, and contemporaneous, providing sufficient detail to allow another veterinarian to continue the care of the patient. (paraphrased)
clauses.implication: Salvia must ensure all SOAP notes include the author's identity, timestamp of entry, and clinical reasoning, ensuring continuity of care.

clauses.title: Patient Identification and History
clauses.text: The medical record must contain the patient's name, signalment (age, breed, sex), and owner contact information. (paraphrased)
clauses.implication: Salvia intake forms must mandate these fields before a clinical note can be generated.

clauses.title: Controlled Substance Records
clauses.text: Registrants must maintain a complete and accurate record of each substance manufactured, received, sold, delivered, or otherwise disposed of. (paraphrased)
clauses.implication: Salvia drug_register must track inventory balances, witness signatures for Schedule II/III drugs, and link usage to specific patient treatment records.

clauses.title: Informed Consent
clauses.text: Written informed consent must be obtained for all surgical procedures and euthanasia, including a discussion of risks and a written cost estimate. (paraphrased)
clauses.implication: Salvia consent_form must include a mandatory cost estimate field and a digital signature capture for the owner.

clauses.title: Anesthesia and Analgesia Logging
clauses.text: Records must include the drugs administered, dosages, routes, and the patient's vital signs monitored during the procedure. (paraphrased)
clauses.implication: Salvia treatment_record must provide structured fields for anesthesia monitoring intervals and drug administration details.

clauses.title: Locum and Staff Attribution
clauses.text: All medical entries must be attributable to the specific veterinarian or staff member providing the service, including their license number. (paraphrased)
clauses.implication: Salvia must enforce user authentication and append the practitioner's credentials to every generated record.

fullName: Federation of State Boards of Physical Therapy
summary: The FSBPT provides the Model Practice Act and standards for physical therapy regulation across US jurisdictions, ensuring safe, ethical, and competent practice through standardized record-keeping and supervision requirements.
longSummary:
The Federation of State Boards of Physical Therapy (FSBPT) serves as the primary resource for state licensing boards in the United States. While individual state boards retain legal authority for licensure, the FSBPT Model Practice Act serves as the gold standard for defining the scope of practice, supervision requirements for physical therapist assistants (PTAs), and the essential components of clinical documentation.

Compliance with FSBPT standards requires that records be contemporaneous, accurate, and reflective of the clinical reasoning process. Documentation must clearly delineate the patient's baseline status, the intervention plan, the rationale for manual therapy or exercise prescription, and the patient's response to treatment. Because regulatory oversight is state-specific, Salvia ensures that records are attributable to the individual clinician via their license number and that all interventions are documented in a manner that supports continuity of care and audit readiness.

Salvia integrates these standards by enforcing structured SOAP note formats and ensuring that all clinical forms—from intake assessments to discharge summaries—capture the necessary data points required by state practice acts. By maintaining a robust audit trail and ensuring all entries are signed and dated, Salvia helps clinics meet the rigorous documentation standards expected during state board audits.

clauses.title: Documentation of Care
clauses.text: A physical therapist shall document all patient encounters in a timely, accurate, and legible manner, including the plan of care, interventions provided, and the patient's response.
clauses.implication: Salvia must enforce a timestamp for every entry that reflects the actual time of the encounter, separate from the time of data entry, to ensure the record is contemporaneous.

clauses.title: Clinical Reasoning and Rationale
clauses.text: Documentation must include the clinical reasoning for the selected interventions and the rationale for the progression or modification of the treatment plan.
clauses.implication: Salvia forms must include mandatory fields for clinical rationale, specifically linking manual therapy or exercise prescription to the patient's functional goals.

clauses.title: Supervision of Personnel
clauses.text: The physical therapist is responsible for the documentation of services provided by physical therapist assistants and must co-sign or review entries to ensure compliance with the plan of care.
clauses.implication: Salvia must support multi-clinician attribution, allowing for clear identification of the treating PTA and the supervising PT, including their respective license numbers.

clauses.title: Informed Consent
clauses.text: The practitioner must obtain and document informed consent from the patient or legal representative prior to initiating treatment, detailing the risks, benefits, and alternatives.
clauses.implication: Salvia's consent_form must be e-signed and stored as a permanent part of the patient's record, with a clear audit trail showing the date and scope of consent.

clauses.title: Outcome Measurement
clauses.text: The plan of care shall be supported by objective, validated outcome measures captured at baseline and at periodic intervals to demonstrate progress.
clauses.implication: Salvia must integrate standardized scales (e.g., NPRS, ODI, LEFS) and track changes over the episode of care to satisfy audit requirements for medical necessity.

clauses.title: Record Retention
clauses.text: Patient records shall be maintained securely for a period defined by state law, typically no less than seven years, ensuring confidentiality and accessibility.
clauses.implication: Salvia must provide secure, encrypted storage with automated retention policies that prevent premature deletion of clinical records.

summary: The NBCE and state chiropractic boards mandate rigorous, contemporaneous, and evidence-based documentation for all chiropractic adjustments and clinical interventions.
longSummary:
The National Board of Chiropractic Examiners (NBCE) establishes the standards for clinical competency, while individual state chiropractic boards enforce the specific record-keeping and scope-of-practice regulations. These bodies require that every patient encounter be documented with sufficient detail to justify the medical necessity of the treatment, including spinal analysis, adjustment techniques, and patient response.

Compliance requires that records are contemporaneous, legible, and attributable to the specific provider. Documentation must include a clear intake assessment, a defined treatment plan with measurable goals, and validated outcome measures to track progress over the episode of care. Failure to maintain these standards can lead to disciplinary action, billing audits, and loss of licensure.

Salvia automates the capture of these requirements by ensuring that every SOAP note, spinal screening, and treatment record includes the necessary clinical rationale and provider attribution. By structuring data around validated outcome measures and standardized adjustment terminology, Salvia provides the audit trail necessary to satisfy state board inspections and insurance billing requirements.

clauses.title: Contemporaneous Documentation
clauses.text: All clinical records must be created at the time of the encounter or as soon as reasonably possible, reflecting the patient's condition and the provider's clinical reasoning.
clauses.implication: Salvia must timestamp the creation and any subsequent edits to the record, ensuring the "date of service" is distinct from the "date of entry."

clauses.title: Medical Necessity
clauses.text: Documentation must clearly establish the medical necessity for chiropractic care, including the diagnosis, the treatment plan, and the expected outcomes.
clauses.implication: Salvia must prompt for the clinical rationale behind every adjustment and ensure the treatment plan is linked to specific, measurable patient goals.

clauses.title: Informed Consent
clauses.text: Chiropractors must obtain and document informed consent, including the risks, benefits, and alternatives to the proposed chiropractic treatment.
clauses.implication: Salvia must use a structured consent form that captures the patient's acknowledgment of risks, specifically regarding spinal manipulation.

clauses.title: Spinal Analysis and Imaging
clauses.text: Records must document the specific spinal segments analyzed, the findings of the analysis, and the justification for any imaging requested.
clauses.implication: Salvia must provide fields for recording segmental subluxation or dysfunction and a clear justification section for diagnostic imaging.

clauses.title: Outcome Assessment
clauses.text: Practitioners must utilize validated outcome measures to track the efficacy of the treatment plan and justify the continuation of care.
clauses.implication: Salvia must integrate standardized outcome measure forms (e.g., Oswestry, NDI) at baseline and regular intervals to demonstrate clinical progress.

clauses.title: Provider Attribution
clauses.text: All entries must be signed, dated, and attributable to the specific licensed provider who performed the service.
clauses.implication: Salvia must enforce user-level authentication and append the provider's NPI or license number to every finalized record.

fullName: National Board for Certification in Occupational Therapy
summary: The NBCOT Practice Standards define the professional responsibilities and record-keeping expectations for Occupational Therapists in the United States.
longSummary:
The National Board for Certification in Occupational Therapy (NBCOT) serves as the national credentialing body for occupational therapy professionals in the United States. While state regulatory boards hold the legal authority for licensure, the NBCOT Practice Standards provide the national benchmark for professional conduct, clinical reasoning, and documentation. These standards ensure that OTs deliver safe, effective, and evidence-based care across all practice settings.

Documentation is a critical component of the NBCOT standards, requiring OTs to maintain records that are accurate, timely, and reflective of the clinical reasoning process. Records must demonstrate the necessity of services, the patient's response to intervention, and the attainment of functional goals. Because OTs often work in interdisciplinary environments, records must be clear enough to facilitate continuity of care and demonstrate compliance with both federal and state-specific regulations.

Salvia integrates these standards by ensuring that every clinical record—from initial intake and functional capacity assessments to discharge summaries—is structured to capture the required clinical rationale and outcome measures. By enforcing contemporaneous documentation and providing a clear audit trail, Salvia helps practitioners meet the NBCOT requirement for accountability and professional integrity.

clauses.title: Practice Standards - Professional Conduct
clauses.text: The OT must provide services in accordance with the laws and regulations of the jurisdiction and adhere to the NBCOT Practice Standards.
clauses.implication: Salvia must surface the clinician's credentials and state license number on all documentation to ensure compliance with jurisdictional requirements.

clauses.title: Practice Standards - Service Delivery
clauses.text: The OT must provide services that are based on the best available evidence and are consistent with the client's needs and goals.
clauses.implication: Salvia must prompt for evidence-based outcome measures (e.g., COPM, AMPS) during intake and review to justify the treatment plan.

clauses.title: Practice Standards - Documentation
clauses.text: The OT must maintain documentation that is accurate, timely, and reflects the clinical reasoning and the services provided.
clauses.implication: Salvia must enforce contemporaneous logging and provide structured fields for clinical reasoning, preventing "copy-paste" notes that lack individualization.

clauses.title: Practice Standards - Communication
clauses.text: The OT must communicate effectively with the client, family, and other professionals involved in the care.
clauses.implication: Salvia must include a dedicated section for interdisciplinary communication and referral tracking to ensure continuity of care.

clauses.title: Practice Standards - Informed Consent
clauses.text: The OT must ensure the client or their representative is fully informed of the risks, benefits, and alternatives to treatment.
clauses.implication: Salvia must use a structured consent widget that captures the specific scope of treatment and the client's signature/date.

clauses.title: Practice Standards - Professional Development
clauses.text: The OT must maintain competence through ongoing professional development and evidence-based practice.
clauses.implication: Salvia should provide audit reports that help the clinician review their own documentation quality and outcome trends over time.
